title: A nice house — adjectives come after
goal: Put nouns and adjectives in Vietnamese order (the reverse of English), use the pointing words *này / kia / đó*, and measure degree with *rất, lắm, quá, hơi, khá*.
bekal: place the adjective **after** its noun: "room big", not "big room"
point at things with *này*, *kia*, *đó* — which also go after the noun

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Xem phòng trọ
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a rented room near campus. The landlady opens the door and shows him around.

lines.speaker: Bà chủ:
lines.text: Mời anh vào. Đây là phòng trọ.
lines.id: Please come in. This is the room for rent.
lines.literal: invite older-brother enter. here be room rent.
lines.baca: Mời ang vào. Dây là fòng chọ.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Oh, this room is so big!

lines.speaker: Bà chủ:
lines.text: Vâng, phòng rộng và sạch. Cửa sổ lớn, rất sáng.
lines.id: Yes, the room is big and clean. The window is large, very bright.

lines.baca: Vâng, fòng zộng và sạk. Kửa sổ lớn, zất sáng.

lines.text: Còn phòng kia thì sao ạ?

lines.text: Cái bàn kia hơi cũ. Có bàn mới không ạ?

notes: **The adjective stands AFTER its noun** — *phòng rộng* (room big), *bàn mới* (table new), *cửa sổ lớn* (window big). That's the reverse of English (*a big window*), and it's the one ordering habit you will have to retrain. The good news: it's completely regular — the describing word always follows.

**There is no *là* before an adjective.** *Phòng này rộng* — not *phòng này là rộng*. Vietnamese adjectives behave like verbs: "the room bigs", so to speak. They stand on their own with no linking word at all.

**Này, kia, đó also stand after.** *Phòng này* = this room, *phòng kia* = that room (over there, visible), *phòng đó* = that room (the one just mentioned). With an adjective as well, the pointing word goes last: *cái bàn mới này* = this new table (literally "table new this").

**Thì sao? means "what about…?" or "and then?"** and is used to move the conversation on to the next thing: *Còn phòng kia thì sao?* = "And what about that room?". The little word *thì* inside it means "then, in that case" — you'll meet it again in Unit 18.

**Không … đâu softens a denial into "not … at all".** *Không ồn đâu!* isn't just "not noisy" but "don't worry, it's not noisy at all" — it reassures. Its opposite is *có … chứ*: *Có chứ!* = "Of course there is!", confirming with slight impatience because the answer is obvious.

**Đi at the end of a sentence turns it into a friendly invitation or nudge**: *lấy đi!* = "go ahead, take it!", *ăn đi!* = "eat up!". Don't confuse it with *đi* meaning "go" — the difference is position: before a verb it means go; at the end of the sentence it means "go on, …!".

grammars.title: Noun order: the thing described comes first
body: Vietnamese puts **the thing being described first and the describing word after**. English does the opposite. This table lines up Vietnamese, a word-for-word rendering and normal English, so you can see exactly what flips.
after: ⚠️ The only group that stands **in front** is **numbers and classifiers**: *hai cái bàn* (two tables) — just like English "two pieces of furniture". Unit 4 covers it fully.
Because adjectives behave like verbs, they can be negated directly with *không* and questioned directly with *có … không?*: *Phòng này **không** rộng.* / *Phòng này **có** rộng **không**?*

grammars.title: Này, kia, đó, ấy — four pointing fingers
body: English has just "this" and "that". Vietnamese splits "that" in two: the one **you can see over there** and the one **we just talked about**.

after: ⚠️ Keep **này** (attached after a noun) apart from **đây** (standing alone as a noun). *Phòng này đẹp* = "this room is nice"; *Đây là phòng* = "this is a room". Swapping them is the most common beginner mistake you'll hear.
*Ấy* feels softer and appears more in writing; *đó* is heard more in conversation. At A1 just use *đó*, and simply **recognize** *ấy* when you read it.

blocks.text: Learn them in pairs, so each sitting gives you two words at once — and your tones get practice side by side.

⚠️ *Xấu* carries two meanings — "ugly" for looks and "bad" for character or quality. And *tốt* is used for things and people, while the taste of food takes another word: *ngon* (tasty). Don't praise food with *tốt*; it sounds like you're rating its nutritional value.

sections.title: Measuring degree: five weights on the scale

blocks.text: Notice that the ones **in front** (*hơi, khá, rất*) sound descriptive and a little cool, while the ones **after** (*lắm, quá*) sound like they come from the heart. That's why spontaneous compliments almost always use *quá* or *lắm*, and calm assessments use *rất*.

blocks.title: Quá has two faces
items: **After** an adjective, *quá* is admiration: *Đẹp quá!* = "So beautiful!" The tone is positive, and this is the use you'll hear all day long.

**Before** an adjective, *quá* means "too" and sounds like a complaint: *quá đắt* = "too expensive". Compare *đắt quá!* ("so expensive!", still open to bargaining) with *quá đắt* ("overpriced", already saying no). One word, two positions, two moods.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
Fill in *hơi*, *rất*, *lắm* or *quá* — watch the position.

items: This room is big and clean.
That table is a bit old.
